title: Python (Interpreted, Multi-Paradigm)
description: Python is an interpreted, dynamically typed language emphasizing readability, with significant whitespace and a vast standard library. It dominates data science, scripting, automation, and education, and serves as this database's demo language. Its reference implementation is CPython; PyPy offers a JIT alternative.
demo:
print('hello from Python', __import__('sys').version.split()[0])
squares = [x*x for x in range(6)]
print('squares:', squares)
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example:
print('hello from Python 3.x')
squares = [x*x for x in range(6)]
print('squares:', squares)

title: C (Compiled, Procedural)
description: C is a compiled procedural language from Bell Labs (1972) giving close-to-hardware control with manual memory management. Operating systems, embedded firmware, and language runtimes are written in it. Its example below shows the canonical hello-world; the demo runs the equivalent logic in Python since a C toolchain is not assumed.
demo:
print('C hello-world:')
print('#include <stdio.h>\nint main(){printf("hello\\n");return 0;}')
print('equivalent running now: hello')
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Haskell (Functional, Lazy)
description: Haskell is a purely functional, lazily evaluated language: functions have no side effects, and values compute only when needed. It pioneered monads, type classes, and equational reasoning adopted across the industry. The demo below runs Haskell-style thinking — map, filter, fold — in Python.
demo:
nums = range(10)
result = sum(x*x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0)
print('Haskell-style (map/filter/fold) sum of even squares:', result)
print('-- haskell: sum [x^2 | x <- [0..9], even x]')
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('-- Haskell: sum [x^2 | x <- [0..9], even x]  (pure, lazy)')

title: Prolog (Logic Programming)
description: Prolog is a logic programming language: you declare facts and rules, and the engine proves queries by search with backtracking. It powers expert systems, natural-language parsing, and symbolic AI. The demo emulates a tiny Prolog-style family database with Python relations.
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('% Prolog: facts + rules; queries proved by search + backtracking')

title: SQL (Declarative Query)
description: SQL is a declarative domain-specific language for relational databases: you describe the result set, and the engine plans the execution. Born at IBM in the 1970s and standardized as ISO SQL, it remains the universal data language. The demo runs the same query logic over Python data.
demo:
rows = [{'name':'a','v':3},{'name':'b','v':7},{'name':'b','v':2}]
res = sorted([r['name'] for r in rows if r['v'] > 4])
print('SQL: SELECT name FROM t WHERE v > 4 ->', res)
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('SQL: SELECT name FROM t WHERE v > 4  (declarative: describe, not instruct)')

title: Bash (Shell Scripting)
description: Bash is the Bourne-again shell scripting language gluing Unix systems together: pipelines, redirection, process control, and text processing. Deployment scripts, cron jobs, and build automation run on it. The demo shows the pipeline pattern in Python.
demo:
words = 'the quick brown fox'.split()
print('bash: echo ... | tr a-z A-Z | wc -w')
print('result:', ' '.join(w.upper() for w in words), '| words:', len(words))
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('bash: echo ... | tr a-z A-Z | wc -w  (pipelines + text processing)')

title: x86 Assembly
description: x86 assembly is human-readable machine code: mnemonics like MOV, ADD, and JMP map nearly one-to-one to CPU instructions over registers and memory. It is used for bootloaders, drivers, and performance-critical kernels. The demo prints a real add-two-numbers routine and runs the equivalent arithmetic.
demo:
print('mov eax, 40 / add eax, 2 / ret   ; eax = 42')
print('executed equivalent: 40 + 2 =', 40 + 2)
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('; x86: mov eax, 40 | add eax, 2 | ret  -> eax = 42')

title: Machine Code (Raw Bytes)
description: Machine code is the raw bytes the CPU fetches and executes — opcodes plus operands, with no symbols at all. The demo shows real x86-64 bytes for a tiny function and decodes them by hand, then runs the equivalent. Disassemblers and debuggers translate these bytes back into assembly for humans.
demo:
code = bytes([0xB8, 0x2A, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0xC3])
print('bytes:', code.hex(' '))
print('decode: B8 2A000000 = mov eax, 0x2a (42); C3 = ret')
print('equivalent result: 42')
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('machine code: B8 2A 00 00 00 C3  (mov eax,42; ret) — raw CPU bytes')

title: JVM Bytecode
description: JVM bytecode is the stack-based intermediate code Java, Kotlin, and Scala compile to, executed by the Java Virtual Machine with JIT compilation to native code. Instructions like iconst, iadd, and invokevirtual manipulate an operand stack. The demo emulates a tiny stack machine adding two numbers.
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('JVM bytecode: iconst_5, iadd, ... — stack-based, JIT-compiled')

title: Regular Expressions (Pattern DSL)
description: Regular expressions are a domain-specific language for describing text patterns, implemented by finite automata. They power search, validation, and lexing across every language. The demo compiles a real email-ish pattern and tests it — this is a genuinely runnable regex example.
demo:
import re
pat = re.compile(r'^[\w.]+@[\w.]+\.[a-z]{2,}$')
for s in ['user@example.com', 'not-an-email']:
    print(s, '->', bool(pat.match(s)))
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.

title: HTML/CSS (Markup & Style)
description: HTML is the markup language structuring web documents (elements, attributes, nesting); CSS is its companion style language (selectors, cascade, box model). Together with JavaScript they are the web platform. The demo prints a minimal valid page skeleton and a styled rule.
demo:
print('

Hello

styled by: h1 { color: navy; }') print('markup = structure; CSS = presentation; JS = behavior')
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.

title: Verilog (Hardware Description)
description: Verilog is a hardware description language: it describes digital circuits — modules, wires, registers, clocks — that synthesize into actual chip layouts or run on FPGAs. Unlike software, its statements model parallel hardware. The demo prints a 2-to-1 multiplexer and simulates its truth table.
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('// Verilog: assign y = sel ? b : a;  (describes parallel hardware)')

title: GLSL (Shader Language)
description: GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language) is a C-like language running on the GPU: vertex shaders transform geometry, fragment shaders compute per-pixel color in massive parallel. Every 3-D game and GPU effect uses shaders. The demo shows a fragment shader turning UV coordinates into a gradient and computes the same gradient on CPU.
demo:
print('vec3 col = vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5); // fragment shader gradient')
print('cpu gradient sample:', [(round(x/4, 2), round(y/4, 2)) for x in range(2) for y in range(2)][:4])
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('// GLSL fragment: vec3(uv.x, uv.y, 0.5) — runs per-pixel on the GPU')

title: Brainfuck (Esoteric)
description: Brainfuck is an esoteric language with only eight commands operating on a tape of memory cells — Turing-complete in minimalism, used to explore computation's essence. The demo includes a real Brainfuck interpreter and runs an actual Brainfuck program that prints 'Hi'. This is genuinely runnable esoteric code.
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.

title: JSON/YAML (Data Formats)
description: JSON and YAML are data-serialization formats, not programming languages, but they are code every system reads: JSON is the web's data interchange format (derived from JavaScript literals), YAML its human-friendly superset for configuration. The demo round-trips real structured data through JSON.
demo:
import json
data = {'name': 'widget', 'tags': ['a', 'b'], 'spec': {'mass': 1.5}}
text = json.dumps(data)
print('serialized:', text)
print('round-trip ok:', json.loads(text) == data)
provenance: Public reference: official language documentation and standard computing references; verified 2026-10-21.
language_example: print('JSON: {"name": "widget"} — the web\'s data interchange code')
